# PL/SQL Cursors

A cursor is a named handle over a result set that procedural code walks a row at a time. The whole
subject reduces to three questions: **who closes it, can it write back to the row it is sitting on,
and is row-at-a-time the right shape at all.**

## Implicit versus explicit — a real choice, not a style preference

`02_cursors.sql` in [[oracle-database-laboratories]] opens with the rule:

> "Cursor FOR loops open, fetch and close automatically and cannot leak. Explicit OPEN / FETCH /
> CLOSE is only worth the extra code when the loop needs to stop early -- and then the CLOSE has to
> be written on every path out, including the exception path."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/03_plsql/02_cursors.sql, 2026-07-25

And the file then demonstrates the cost it just described. The "five hungriest cats" block exits after
five fetches, so it *must* use an explicit cursor — and it carries a `WHEN OTHERS` handler that tests
`%ISOPEN`, closes, and re-raises. An unclosed cursor holds its slot for the whole session; the leak is
silent until the session hits `OPEN_CURSORS`.

This is the same shape as any resource with a lifetime: the convenient form is convenient precisely
because it removes a path you would otherwise have to handle by hand.

## `FOR UPDATE` and `WHERE CURRENT OF`

Declaring a cursor `FOR UPDATE OF col` locks the selected rows for the transaction and lets the loop
body write back with `WHERE CURRENT OF cursor_name` — updating exactly the row the cursor is on,
without re-stating the predicate and without re-finding the row by key.

The lab uses it for an iterative pass: raise every ration by 10 %, capped at the function's ceiling,
repeatedly, until the herd total clears a threshold. The termination condition is the interesting part
— it exits when **a pass changes nothing**, not when the target is met, because once every cat sits at
its ceiling the target may simply be unreachable and a `WHILE total <= …` loop would spin forever.
Loop-termination-on-no-progress is a general fixpoint idiom, not a database one.

## Cursor attributes

`%FOUND`, `%NOTFOUND`, `%ROWCOUNT`, `%ISOPEN` on the cursor; `%ROWTYPE` to declare a record matching
its projection and `%TYPE` to declare a variable matching one column. The last two matter beyond
convenience: they make the block survive a column widening in the table without an edit.

## When row-at-a-time is the wrong shape

The cross-tabulation exercise (bands down the side, functions across the top, gender splitting each
band) is built by aggregating **once** into an associative array — `TABLE OF NUMBER INDEX BY
VARCHAR2(60)` — and then formatting from memory. Driving the report straight from SQL would issue one
query per cell.

One trap comes with it: reading an associative array at a key that was never assigned raises
`NO_DATA_FOUND` rather than returning `NULL`, so every read in the block goes through an `EXISTS`
helper instead of through `NVL` — see [[plsql-exception-handling]] for why that is a raise and not a
return value.

**The rule the file is teaching:** a cursor loop that issues a query per iteration is a join written
badly. Aggregate once, then iterate over the result.
